opus-5.5.text:
Static benchmarks were built for a world where a model answers a question in a few seconds, and you check whether the answer is right. That's still useful, but it breaks down once models can work on a task for hours, days, or eventually weeks.

The first problem is saturation. A fixed set of questions gets solved, sometimes faster than anyone expected, and then it stops telling you much. You end up in a constant cycle of building harder benchmarks just to keep up.

The second problem is more fundamental: a static benchmark measures the final answer, not the process. When a model works over a long horizon, what matters is how it gets there. Does it plan well? Does it recover when something goes wrong? Does it know when to ask for help, or when it's stuck? Does it stay coherent across thousands of steps? A single score at the end hides almost all of that.

Third, real work isn't a closed-form question. In actual jobs, the task is often underspecified, the environment changes, and there are other people involved: feedback, shifting requirements, a manager who wants something slightly different than what they first asked for. Static benchmarks freeze all of that out. So you can get a model that looks amazing on paper but doesn't translate into real economic value, or the reverse, a model that's more useful than its scores suggest.

And then there's cost and grading. If a task takes a model a week, you can't run it thousands of times cheaply, and you often can't grade it automatically. You need expert humans to judge whether the output is actually good, the way you'd evaluate a professional's work product. That's expensive and slow, but I think it's where evaluation has to go.

So the direction I'm excited about is evals grounded in real-world tasks: work that actual professionals do, judged by experts in those fields, and increasingly interactive, long-horizon environments where we can watch how the model behaves over time, not just whether it gets the last answer right. The question shifts from "does it know the answer?" to "can it actually do the job?"

r001.rationale: It says static benchmarks measure only the final answer and hide how models plan, recover, and stay coherent across thousands of steps, addressing sustained useful work over long horizons.

r002.rationale: It notes that week-long tasks and expert grading make evaluation expensive and slow, identifying evaluation time as a constraint.

r003.rationale: It proposes professional real-world tasks and interactive long-horizon environments, but does not describe observing tasks people accomplish with models in production.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the core problem is that static benchmarks were designed for a world where you ask a model a question and it gives you an answer, and you check whether the answer is right. And that was a fine abstraction when the unit of work was a single response. But when you're talking about a model that's going to work on something for days or weeks, the thing you actually care about is not "did it get the right answer at the end," it's the whole trajectory. Did it make reasonable decisions when it hit something ambiguous? Did it notice when it was going down the wrong path and recover? Did it know when to stop and ask for help versus when to just push through?

And a static benchmark basically can't see any of that. You get a scalar at the end, and that scalar is compressing an enormous amount of information about what happened along the way.

There are a few more specific problems I'd point to. One is that the longer the task, the more the outcome depends on the environment you put the model in, rather than the model itself. What tools does it have? What does the feedback loop look like? Can it run tests? Can it browse? And so two labs can report numbers on the "same" benchmark and be measuring very different things, because the scaffolding matters as much as the model once the horizon gets long enough.

Another is saturation and contamination, which everyone talks about, but it gets worse with long-horizon tasks because the tasks are expensive to build. If it takes a domain expert a week to construct a realistic task that would take a model days to complete, you're not going to have ten thousand of them. You're going to have a few hundred at most. And a few hundred tasks is not a lot of statistical power, and it's also a small enough set that it can leak into training data or get overfit to pretty quickly.

And then the one I think is most underrated is that static benchmarks have a fixed notion of what "done" means. In real long-horizon work, the goal often shifts as you learn things. You start a project, you discover the original spec was wrong, you renegotiate. A model that rigidly executes the original instruction for two weeks is actually failing, even if it "completes the task." But a benchmark with a fixed grader will score that as a success.

So the direction I think evaluation has to move is toward things that look more like how we evaluate people doing real work. More emphasis on the process, not just the output. Graders that are themselves adaptive or human-in-the-loop. Tasks that are drawn from real economic activity, where we can compare against what an actual expert produced, rather than against a reference answer we wrote in advance. And honestly, a lot more humility about what any single number means.

r001.rationale: It says static benchmarks miss the trajectory of work over days or weeks, including decisions, recovery, and knowing when to ask for help.

r002.rationale: It does not identify the need for timely evaluation results as a constraint.

r003.rationale: It proposes tasks based on real economic activity and comparison with expert work, but does not describe observing tasks people accomplish with models in production.

astra-6.text:
I think static benchmarks are useful, but they’re a snapshot. You give a model a well-defined task, and you measure whether it gets the right answer. When a model is working for days or weeks, the question becomes: can it sustain progress toward a goal?

That involves things that are hard to capture in a single score. Can it recognize that an approach isn’t working and change course? Can it recover from a mistake instead of building on it? Can it ask for clarification when it needs it, and incorporate new information as the task evolves?

You also have to evaluate the process over time. A model might produce a good final artifact but require so much human intervention that it hasn’t actually saved you much work. Or it might make an early mistake whose consequences only become apparent much later.

So I’d think of static benchmarks as one part of the picture. We also need evaluations that let the model operate over longer horizons and measure whether it delivers a useful outcome, how reliably it does that, and how much oversight it needs along the way.

r002.rationale: It does not identify timely evaluation results as a constraint.

r003.rationale: It calls for longer-horizon evaluations but does not describe observing tasks people accomplish with models in production.

sol-6.1.text:
Static benchmarks give you a snapshot: can the model solve this particular problem, usually in a fairly constrained setting? But if you want a model to work for days or weeks, you care about the whole trajectory. Can it make a plan, recognize when that plan isn’t working, recover from mistakes, and keep making progress toward the actual goal?

A model might do very well on individual tasks and still struggle to put those capabilities together reliably over a long period. Small errors can compound. It might lose track of a constraint, or spend a lot of time pursuing something that isn’t useful. A final score doesn’t necessarily tell you where that happened or why.

So static benchmarks are still useful, but we also need evaluations that let models operate over longer horizons, with feedback and changing conditions, and measure whether they actually get the work done. The hard part is making those evaluations realistic while keeping them reproducible and interpretable.

r001.rationale: It says static benchmarks provide only a snapshot and do not show whether a model can make sustained progress toward a goal over days or weeks.

r002.rationale: It mentions keeping long-horizon evaluations reproducible and interpretable, but does not identify timely evaluation results as a constraint.

r003.rationale: It calls for evaluations over longer horizons, but does not describe observing tasks people accomplish with models in production.
